title: Variationally correct physics-informed operator learning for nonlinear partial differential equations
authors: Yuan Qiu, Wolfgang Dahmen, Peng Chen
abstract: Physics-informed operator learning trains neural operators on the residual of a parametric partial differential equation (PDE) instead of labeled solution data, but its reliability depends on a variationally correct residual: one that is equivalent to the error in a norm dictated by the equation, the PDE-compliant norm. For nonlinear equations written as first-order systems, we prove that the first-order system least-squares residual is equivalent to the error in this norm near a solution branch if the linearized residual is stable and the residual derivative is Lipschitz continuous, possibly in a norm stronger than the error norm. We verify these conditions for monotone reaction, solution- and gradient-dependent diffusion, and compressible Neo-Hookean hyperelasticity. The stability mechanisms vary across these classes, as do the regions where the equivalence holds, from arbitrary bounded sets to a neighborhood of the branch. In a conforming finite element space, we show that the loss excess of a state near the finite element solution is equivalent to its squared distance from that solution. We use this loss to train a reduced basis neural operator with values in this space, with solution snapshots needed only for the basis and the loss and its symbolically derived gradient assembled by the finite element library. At inference, this loss estimates the error. Numerically, the square root of the loss excess tracks the error within factors comparable to those of the linear case, and the operator achieves higher accuracy in the PDE-compliant norm than grid-based baselines evaluated in the same finite element space.

infographic.key_insight: A variationally correct first-order least-squares residual makes physics-informed operator learning locally error-equivalent in the PDE-compliant norm.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For nonlinear mechanics, including compressible Neo-Hookean hyperelasticity, this provides a principled training objective and an inference-time error indicator.
method: Establish residual–error equivalence using linearized stability and Lipschitz continuity of the residual derivative.
Train a reduced-basis neural operator in a conforming finite element space, using solution snapshots only to construct the basis.
Assemble the residual loss and its symbolically derived gradient with a finite element library.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical tests show that the square root of loss excess tracks error within factors comparable to the linear case, while the operator outperforms grid-based baselines in the PDE-compliant norm.
infographic.watch_item: The guarantees depend on stability and regularity assumptions and may hold only near a solution branch, rather than globally.
infographic.paper_title: Variationally correct physics-informed operator learning for nonlinear partial differential equations

title: Fuse-PINN: Combining Finite Element Methods and Physics-Informed Neural Networks to enable massively parallel simulations of non-linear PDEs
authors: Stanislas Pamela, Nicolas Pailliez, Emmanuel Franck, Victor Michel-Dansac, Laurent Navoret, Vignesh Gopakumar
abstract: Research in the domain of Physics-Informed Neural Networks applied to PDE modelling has advanced significantly in recent years, providing a wide ecosystem of novel methods. However, one frequent limitation is the inability of PINNs to scale out on High-Performance Computing architectures to address more ambitious challenges, particularly non-linear physics models with turbulent dynamics in large spatial domains. Typical studies restrain demonstrations to toy models with simple physics equations, few variables, and rarely any complex non-linear dynamics evolved over long timescales. Part of the AI community has even adopted the idea that "PINNs don't scale". This work proves otherwise. We present a mathematically robust formulation of Finite-Element-Method for Neural Networks (FEM-NN) implemented into a comprehensive, modular framework: Fuse-PINN. This formulation provides the basis for a sclable parallelisation of Physics-Informed Neural Networks on GPU-based HPC systems. Furthermore, an Energy Natural Gradient Descent optimiser is implemented to allow high-precision convergence. Fuse-PINN is demonstrated on physics models relevant to Magnetic Confinement Fusion, including non-linear convective models with fine-scale dynamics. Near-perfect scaling is achieved on multi-GPU runs with increasing problem size.

infographic.key_insight: Fuse-PINN combines finite-element methods with physics-informed neural networks to enable scalable multi-GPU simulations of nonlinear PDEs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a route to large-domain, fine-scale nonlinear physics simulation on GPU-based HPC systems, demonstrated for magnetic-confinement fusion rather than solid mechanics.
method: Formulates a finite-element method for neural networks (FEM-NN).
Implements FEM-NN in a modular framework for parallel GPU execution.
Uses Energy Natural Gradient Descent for high-precision convergence.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports near-perfect scaling as problem size increases across multiple GPUs, with demonstrations including nonlinear convective models with fine-scale dynamics.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify GPU counts, accuracy, or speedups over conventional FEM solvers, leaving practical performance gains to be assessed.
infographic.paper_title: Fuse-PINN: Combining Finite Element Methods and Physics-Informed Neural Networks to enable massively parallel simulations of non-linear PDEs

title: Mesoscale Neural Operators: Learning Nonlinear Constitutive Laws from Molecular Dynamics for Scalable Fracture Predictions
authors: Yue Yu, Jihong Wang, Stewart Silling, Ziwei Yang
abstract: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations can capture the nanoscale physics of fracture at the atomistic level, but their computational cost prohibits predictions at the length scales and time scales needed for many applications. Machine learning approaches, on the other hand, have been proposed as heuristic surrogates for material fracture, yet they cannot guarantee the physical consistency of the predicted response. To address this shortcoming, we propose the mesoscale neural operator (MNO): a data-driven nonlocal constitutive model that is learned directly from MD loading and displacement data. After training, it can be used in continuum fracture simulations on much larger domains and grid sizes. The key idea of the MNO is to exploit the built-in characteristic length of a nonlocal model, called the horizon, to travel across scales. Physical consistency across scales is obtained by building two structural ingredients into the MNO: a normalized kernel that renders the strain energy density invariant under horizon rescaling, and a rescaled critical bond stretch that keeps the energy release rate consistent across scales. Through tests on synthetic data, we show that the MNO and its learning workflow indeed discover the nonlocal continuum multiscale model in the form of the nonlocal kernel and the nonlinear constitutive relation. We then apply the framework to coarse-grained MD data and find that in a test problem, the learned model matches the MD strain energy density and critical energy release rate within 3%. It also predicts the peak transmitted forces within 6% in out-of-distribution tension tests. As a further demonstration, the model is applied to a plate with 4000 times the area of the training specimens and containing an initial defect. In this problem, the model reproduces the main features of dynamic brittle fracture, including branch and cascading branch networks.

infographic.key_insight: Mesoscale neural operators learn nonlocal constitutive laws from molecular dynamics while preserving strain energy density and fracture energy across horizon rescaling.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach enables continuum fracture simulations on much larger domains and coarser grids than atomistic simulations can afford.
method: Learn a nonlocal kernel and nonlinear constitutive relation from MD loading and displacement data.
Normalize the kernel to preserve strain energy density under horizon rescaling.
Rescale critical bond stretch to maintain consistent fracture energy across scales.
infographic.evidence_signal: Synthetic tests support model recovery; MD-based tests report energy metrics within 3% and out-of-distribution peak forces within 6%, plus a fracture demonstration on a plate with 4,000× the training-specimen area.
infographic.watch_item: The reported tests do not establish generalization to other materials or loading regimes; broader validation is needed before engineering deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Mesoscale Neural Operators: Learning Nonlinear Constitutive Laws from Molecular Dynamics for Scalable Fracture Predictions

title: Scientific Coding with Large Language Models: Evidence from Finite Element Analysis
authors: Erfan Hamdi, Joel Shor, Emma Lejeune
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) offer a potential route to automating scientific programming, but their usefulness depends on consistently producing numerically correct code. We extend FEM-Bench to 17 finite element tasks involving nonlinear and history-dependent mechanics and structural dynamics, and evaluate 15 models on implementation and test generation without execution feedback. The best model succeeds in 87.1% of single-pass implementation trials, but rankings differ between tracks. The leading implementer achieves 49.9% joint test success, while the leading tester reaches 82.6%. For six models, we compare single-pass generation with two agentic harnesses that allow code execution and revision. Agentic execution solves some tasks that never succeeded in single-pass trials and improves consistency on others, but gains vary across models and harnesses, and regressions also occur. Claude Opus 5 with SimpleAgent reaches 96.5% Pass@3, the probability of at least one success in three attempts, but 77.1% Pass$^3$, the probability that all three succeed. No model-harness combination exceeds 78.8% Pass$^3$. To understand why agents submit incorrect code after passing their own checks, we analyze 249 failed agentic trajectories and identify six categories of self-verification failure. The most common are inadequate test coverage (73.1%) and reliance on generic consistency checks (70.3%), and in 28.5% of cases the tests share an error with the implementation. Motivated by these findings, an exploratory configuration with separate coder and tester agents achieves the highest observed scores, with 97.6% Pass@3 and 88.8% Pass$^3$. These results identify consistency across attempts and independent verification as the main obstacles to trusting LLM-generated scientific code.

infographic.key_insight: LLMs can generate correct finite element code, but consistency across attempts and independent verification remain critical barriers to trust.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Automating nonlinear mechanics and structural dynamics coding requires numerical validation beyond passing an agent’s own tests.
method: Extend FEM-Bench to 17 finite element tasks and evaluate 15 models on implementation and test generation.
Compare single-pass generation with two execution-and-revision harnesses for six models.
Analyze 249 failed agentic trajectories and explore separate coder and tester agents.
infographic.evidence_signal: The exploratory coder–tester configuration achieved 97.6% probability of at least one success across three attempts and 88.8% probability that all three succeeded.
infographic.watch_item: Self-tests can falsely reassure: 28.5% of failed agentic trajectories had tests sharing an error with the implementation, and the separate-agent results remain exploratory.
infographic.paper_title: Scientific Coding with Large Language Models: Evidence from Finite Element Analysis

title: A Staggered Discontinuous Galerkin Neural Network Method with a Computable Error Decomposition
authors: Gung-Min Gie, Chang-Yeol Jung, Bongsuk Kwon, Kiwoong Kwon
abstract: We develop a staggered discontinuous Galerkin neural network (SDGNN) method for scalar elliptic problems with a computable error decomposition. The staggered discontinuous Galerkin (SDG) method requires only local continuity of its trial functions and gives a square, inf-sup stable system without stabilization parameters; we carry this structure over to neural networks. Networks defined on the patches of a staggered mesh satisfy the SDG continuity conditions for all values of the network parameters, and the loss is the squared dual norm of the SDG weak residual. We show that the loss is equivalent, with computable constants, to the square of the training error, the distance between the SDG projection of the network and the SDG finite element approximation, so that the full error is bounded by the discretization error, a multiple of the square root of the loss, and the network projection error. The weak residual requires no derivatives of the networks, the boundary and convection terms carry no penalty or stabilization weights, and the scalar trial functions may jump across the midlines of the primal cells. Numerical experiments show that the square root of the loss tracks the error during the training, that prescribed jumps across a square and a circular interface are captured consistently over the initializations, and that the method is more accurate than physics-informed neural networks at the same parameter counts.

infographic.key_insight: SDGNN preserves staggered discontinuous Galerkin structure while providing a computable error decomposition linking the training loss to solution accuracy.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For scalar elliptic simulations relevant to engineering, the method offers an error-aware neural approximation that accommodates prescribed interface jumps.
method: Define patchwise neural networks that satisfy SDG continuity conditions by construction.
Minimize the squared dual norm of the weak residual without network derivatives or penalty and stabilization weights.
Bound total error by discretization error, a computable multiple of the square root of the loss, and network projection error.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments show that the square root of the loss tracks error during training, square and circular interface jumps are captured consistently across initializations, and SDGNN outperforms PINNs at matched parameter counts.
infographic.watch_item: A small training loss alone does not guarantee small total error; discretization and network projection errors must also be controlled.
infographic.paper_title: A Staggered Discontinuous Galerkin Neural Network Method with a Computable Error Decomposition

title: A mesoscale damage model for void nucleation and growth in shock loaded microstructure informed by computer vision
authors: Abhijith Thoopul Anantharanga, Brandon Runnels
abstract: Spallation in ductile materials under high strain rates occurs through the process of void nucleation, growth, and coalescence. Void nucleation is known to depend on factors ranging from microstructural to stress state. The criteria for void nucleation in damage models are stochastic, and microstructural awareness is often neglected. Recently, it was shown that nucleation propensity can be estimated using computer vision. In the present work, this is integrated with a continuum damage model framework for comprehensive simulation of spallation in tantalum under plate impact. Void nucleation probability is governed by a susceptibility field, predicted from grain orientations and grain boundary (GB) energy, with a mechanical barrier set by the local maximum principal stress. This is coupled to a crystal plasticity model within a Lagrangian shock simulation, with microstructure selectively resolved to reduce computational cost. The model is calibrated at a flyer velocity of 196 m/s, where the simulated free surface velocity (FSV) matches experimental measurements of shock arrival, peak state, release and the pullback signal measured in flyer impact experiments, with some deviations confined to the late time ringing. With no further parameter changes, the model transfers to a 214 m/s case and accurately reproduces the FSV. To demonstrate the microstructure-awareness of the nucleation model, a selection of synthetic microstructures is presented for comparison. In the resolved microstructure, voids nucleate predominantly (though not exclusively) at GBs and triple junctions. It is shown that the FSV differs significantly based on the incorporated microstructure, yielding the correct FSV prediction only in the case of representative microstructures.

infographic.key_insight: Computer-vision-informed void nucleation makes a mesoscale damage model sensitive to microstructure and enables prediction of shock-induced spallation in tantalum.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach links grain-scale structure to plate-impact response, supporting microstructure-aware assessment of high-rate material failure.
method: Predict a void-nucleation susceptibility field from grain orientations and grain-boundary energy.
Gate nucleation by local maximum principal stress and model subsequent void growth.
Couple damage to crystal plasticity in a Lagrangian shock simulation with selectively resolved microstructure.
infographic.evidence_signal: Calibrated at 196 m/s flyer velocity, the model reproduced key experimental free-surface velocity features and transferred to 214 m/s without parameter changes.
infographic.watch_item: Accurate predictions depend on representative microstructures, and late-time free-surface velocity ringing showed deviations.
infographic.paper_title: A mesoscale damage model for void nucleation and growth in shock loaded microstructure informed by computer vision

title: Pharmaco-mechanical computational simulation of atherosclerotic arteries: effects of calcium channel blockers on local stress distributions
authors: Sharan Nurani Ramesh, Lea Saßmannshausen, Axel Klawonn, Daniel Balzani
abstract: This paper presents a computational model integrating transmural drug transport, smooth muscle cell contraction, nonlinear anisotropic material behavior, and residual stresses to investigate the effects of calcium channel blockers~(CCBs) on local stress distributions in atherosclerotic arteries. The balance of linear momentum is coupled with a three-dimensional reaction-diffusion equation for the drug transport. Smooth muscle contraction is modeled phenomenologically based on a chemo-mechanical model that incorporates the effects of stretch on intracellular calcium dynamics and calcium sensitization. A novel drug-tissue interaction model is proposed to capture the effects of CCBs on intracellular calcium and thus on smooth muscle contraction. Material parameters are identified by fitting to experimental data from the literature and finite element simulations are conducted on five exemplary atherosclerotic arterial geometries reconstructed from histological cross-sections. Simulation results show that although CCBs reduce the stresses in the media through reduced smooth muscle contraction, they shift load to the fibrous cap, whose stress increases in all five geometries (median of up to 28.9~kPa). This increase varies strongly between plaque morphologies and becomes smaller with lower smooth muscle tone before treatment, lower drug concentrations in the arterial wall and increasing axial pre-stretch. A blood pressure reduction of 10~mmHg already lowers it to a median of at most 3.8~kPa in four of the five geometries. Our findings suggest that CCBs may increase the rupture risk of vulnerable plaques with highly loaded fibrous caps under insufficient blood pressure reduction, which remains to be confirmed experimentally and clinically.

infographic.key_insight: The simulations predict that calcium channel blockers reduce arterial media stress but shift load to the fibrous cap, potentially increasing plaque rupture risk if blood pressure reduction is insufficient.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Coupled drug-transport and arterial-mechanics modeling reveals local stress trade-offs that should be considered when assessing treatment effects on atherosclerotic plaques.
method: Couple 3D reaction–diffusion drug transport with finite element arterial mechanics.
Model calcium-dependent smooth muscle contraction and drug–tissue interactions.
Include nonlinear anisotropic tissue behavior and residual stresses.
infographic.evidence_signal: With material parameters fitted to literature experiments, simulations of five histology-derived geometries predicted fibrous-cap stress increases in all five, with median increases up to 28.9 kPa; a 10 mmHg blood pressure reduction limited median increases to at most 3.8 kPa in four geometries.
infographic.watch_item: The predicted increase in plaque rupture risk remains unconfirmed experimentally and clinically, and evaluation covered only five exemplary geometries.
infographic.paper_title: Pharmaco-mechanical computational simulation of atherosclerotic arteries: effects of calcium channel blockers on local stress distributions

title: Scaled boundary finite elements for FFT-based computational micromechanics
authors: Flavia Gehrig, Carolin Birk, Matti Schneider
abstract: We introduce a matrix-free FFT-based solver for three-dimensional linear elastic homogenization problems discretized by the scaled boundary finite element method (SBFEM) on a voxel grid. Owing to its analytical solution in the radial direction, the SBFEM discretization is inherently softer than fully integrated voxel finite elements, whereas its displacement-based formulation remains symmetric, conforming, and supports arbitrary stiffness anisotropy. These properties make SBFEM an attractive candidate for porous and highly heterogeneous microstructures, where existing voxel-based FFT discretizations offer no generally reliable choice: Reduced-integration hexahedral elements, equivalently the rotated staggered grid discretization, may suffer from hourglass instabilities in the presence of voids, whereas fully integrated hexahedral elements are often too stiff. The proposed discretization uses hexahedral SBFEM cells on the full voxel mesh of a regular periodic grid, retaining the simplicity of a fixed-resolution voxel representation without requiring adaptive mesh coarsening. The main contribution is a preconditioner based on the homogeneous SBFEM stiffness operator. We show that this preconditioner may be applied locally in Fourier space and that the condition number of the preconditioned system is bounded by the material contrast, independently of the grid resolution. This result enables a fully matrix-free implementation of the SBFEM-discretized problem, without assembling or storing the global stiffness matrix. Numerical experiments on a short-fibre reinforced composite, a polyurethane foam and a sand-based binder jet microstructure demonstrate robust convergence and competitive accuracy compared with established voxel discretizations. In particular, SBFEM remains stable for porous microstructures, for which reduced-integration hexahedral elements become unstable.

infographic.key_insight: A matrix-free FFT solver using scaled boundary finite elements offers a softer alternative to fully integrated voxel elements while remaining stable in tested porous microstructures.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method supports elastic homogenization of porous and highly heterogeneous materials on regular voxel grids without assembling or storing a global stiffness matrix.
method: Discretize a periodic voxel grid with hexahedral SBFEM cells and analytical radial solutions.
Apply a homogeneous SBFEM stiffness preconditioner locally in Fourier space.
Bound the preconditioned system’s condition number by material contrast, independently of grid resolution.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests on a short-fibre composite, polyurethane foam, and sand-based binder jet microstructure showed robust convergence and competitive accuracy, including stability where reduced-integration elements became unstable.
infographic.watch_item: The condition-number bound depends on material contrast, so grid independence alone does not guarantee contrast-independent convergence.
infographic.paper_title: Scaled boundary finite elements for FFT-based computational micromechanics

title: Making Plasticity Visible: A Case Study for High-Temperature Exposed Aluminum Alloy
authors: Bakhtiyar Mammadli, Karol Frydrych, Casim Yazici, Azad Mammadli, Kazimierz Skrobas, Siddharth Suman
abstract: Understanding the onset of plastic deformation and the early development of strain localization is essential for characterizing material behavior and identifying failure-prone regions. However, these transitions are not always distinguishable from conventional full-field strain measurements. This study investigates a data- driven framework combining Digital Image Correlation (DIC) and Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to extract temporal and spatial deformation signatures during uniaxial tensile loading. The methodology is evaluated using AA6063-T5 aluminum alloy specimens in the as-received condition and following thermal exposure at 100~$^\circ$C, 200~$^\circ$C, and 300~$^\circ$C. PCA applied to sequential strain fields reveals a characteristic peak in the second principal component projection near the yielding transition, showing agreement with the conventional 0.2\% offset criterion across the investigated conditions. Furthermore, principal component maps extracted from high-temporal-resolution strain fields preceding this transition highlight localized deformation features associated with subsequent failure regions. These features are more clearly distinguishable than competing strain concentrations in the corresponding instantaneous strain maps. The results indicate that PCA-derived deformation signatures remain identifiable despite thermally induced variations in mechanical response. This approach demonstrates the potential of unsupervised dimensionality reduction for extracting physically interpretable information on plastic deformation and early strain localization from experimental full-field measurements.

infographic.key_insight: PCA of full-field strain measurements reveals signatures of yielding and early strain localization that are less distinguishable in instantaneous strain maps.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could help identify plasticity onset and failure-prone regions in aluminum components despite thermal-exposure-induced changes in mechanical response.
method: Measure sequential strain fields during uniaxial tension using Digital Image Correlation (DIC).
Apply unsupervised Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to extract temporal deformation signatures and spatial component maps.
Compare the second-component projection peak with 0.2% offset yielding and inspect pre-transition maps for localization.
infographic.evidence_signal: For AA6063-T5 tested as received and after exposure at 100°C, 200°C, and 300°C, the second-component peak agreed with 0.2% offset yielding, while pre-transition component maps highlighted regions associated with subsequent failure.
infographic.watch_item: Evidence is limited to one alloy under uniaxial tension; robustness to other loading conditions and DIC acquisition settings remains to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Making Plasticity Visible: A Case Study for High-Temperature Exposed Aluminum Alloy

title: Unified constitutive model of body-centered cubic metals informed by discrete dislocation dynamics
authors: Jiarui Zhang, Yin Zhang
abstract: Predicting plastic flow in body-centered cubic metals across temperature and strain-rate regimes requires distinguishing structural resistance from kinetic contributions. Here, we develop a temperature dependent mobility law for screw dislocation, integrating thermal activation theory and relativistic effects. Through discrete dislocation dynamics simulations, uniaxial tension and compression simulations were conducted on configurations with different initial dislocation densities, elucidating the correlation between plastic strain rate and key parameters such as stress, temperature, and dislocation density. Subsequently, a unified constitutive model incorporating temperature and strain rate is derived based on microscopic mechanisms. The model naturally bridges microscopic mechanisms to continuum response, resolving the additivity dilemma by establishing explicit physical criteria for how structural resistances and competing kinetic mechanisms superimpose. Through rigorous bottom-up simulations, we quantitatively capture the crossover point where phonon drag overtakes thermal activation, providing a mechanism-based explanation of anomalous thermal hardening. This work enables physically consistent predictions of strength and creep behavior across broad temperature and strain-rate regimes, advancing beyond phenomenological descriptions toward transparent, mechanism-based alloy design.

infographic.key_insight: A dislocation-informed constitutive model links BCC metal flow to temperature and strain rate while specifying how structural resistance and competing kinetic mechanisms combine.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The model supports mechanism-based prediction of strength and creep across temperature and loading-rate regimes, with potential value for alloy design.
method: Develop a temperature-dependent screw-dislocation mobility law combining thermal activation and relativistic effects.
Run discrete dislocation dynamics tension and compression simulations with varied initial dislocation densities.
Derive a unified constitutive model connecting microscopic mechanisms to continuum plastic flow.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports bottom-up simulations that quantify the crossover from thermal activation to phonon drag and explain anomalous thermal hardening.
infographic.watch_item: Experimental validation and quantitative prediction errors are not reported in the abstract, leaving practical transferability to specific BCC alloys uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: Unified constitutive model of body-centered cubic metals informed by discrete dislocation dynamics

title: Maximum principle preserving approximation of scalar conservation equations with a fractional Laplacian
authors: Andrea Bonito, Jean-Luc Guermond, Murtazo Nazarov
abstract: In this paper, we propose a maximum principle preserving continuous finite element method for scalar conservation laws augmented with a fractional diffusion operator of order $s\in (0,1)$. Conservation laws with fractional diffusion operators arise in a variety of physical models involving anomalous transport and nonlocal regularization, including geophysical flows, plasma physics, and nonlinear acoustics. The fractional Laplacian is approximated using a sinc-quadrature representation, yielding a resolvent-based formulation compatible with continuous finite elements and explicit strong stability preserving Runge--Kutta time integration. A first-order monotone scheme is constructed using graph viscosity and is shown to satisfy a discrete maximum principle under an explicit CFL condition. A high-order extension is obtained via entropy-consistent corrections and convex limiting, achieving second-order accuracy while preserving the maximum principle, and hence positivity, as well as mass conservation in the periodic setting. Numerical experiments, including applications to the Surface Quasi-Geostrophic equation, confirm the second-order accuracy and the robustness of the proposed method on unstructured meshes.

infographic.key_insight: A continuous finite element method achieves second-order accuracy for scalar conservation laws with fractional diffusion while preserving a discrete maximum principle.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method supports physically bounded simulations of anomalous transport and nonlocal diffusion on unstructured meshes.
method: Approximate the fractional Laplacian using sinc quadrature and finite element resolvent solves.
Combine graph viscosity with explicit SSP Runge–Kutta integration for a monotone baseline.
Apply entropy-consistent corrections and convex limiting for maximum-principle-preserving second-order accuracy.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments, including Surface Quasi-Geostrophic applications, confirm second-order accuracy and robustness on unstructured meshes.
infographic.watch_item: Maximum-principle preservation requires an explicit CFL restriction, while fractional diffusion introduces multiple resolvent solves.
infographic.paper_title: Maximum principle preserving approximation of scalar conservation equations with a fractional Laplacian

title: An all-steps-at-once algorithm for time-domain wave propagation in heterogeneous and unbounded media
authors: V. Domínguez, M. Ganesh
abstract: We propose, analyze, and implement a convolution quadrature (CQ) algorithm for transient acoustic waves in an unbounded medium consisting of a heterogeneous domain embedded in free space, where the wave speed may be spatially variable and discontinuous. Multistep CQ, applied to the time-domain solution operator, reduces the evolution problem to a family of Helmholtz problems with damped complex frequencies, which can be solved independently in parallel, all time steps at once. The frequency problems are discretized by an overlapping coupling of finite elements (FEM) on a polygonal/polyhedral domain containing the inhomogeneity, and boundary elements (BEM) on a smooth curve enclosed by that domain, in the region where the medium is homogeneous, which accounts exactly for the unbounded exterior. Neither discretization needs to conform to the geometry of the heterogeneous domain, nor to each other. For the resulting FEM--BEM coupling we prove bounds for the solution operators of the transformed problems that are explicit in the Laplace parameter and the wave speed. These bounds yield convergence of the time discretization for A-stable multistep schemes. We also prove explicit estimates on the exponential decay of the transformed solutions away from the heterogeneity, which show that the correction provided by the BEM part is small but relevant, and cheap to compute: a few GMRES iterations suffice, and the correction is needed only over a fixed range of weakly damped frequencies, beyond which it becomes negligible and can be dropped. Numerical experiments confirm the predicted convergence rates in time and space and explore iterative (multigrid) methods for the interior FEM problems.

infographic.key_insight: Convolution quadrature converts transient acoustic wave propagation in heterogeneous, unbounded media into independent complex-frequency Helmholtz problems that can be solved in parallel.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method supports wave simulations with variable or discontinuous wave speeds while accounting for the unbounded exterior without artificial truncation.
method: Apply A-stable multistep convolution quadrature to solve all time steps through parallel frequency-domain problems.
Couple interior FEM with exterior BEM using overlapping, mutually nonconforming discretizations.
Retain BEM corrections for weakly damped frequencies and omit them where exponential decay makes them negligible.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments confirm predicted temporal and spatial convergence rates and explore multigrid solvers for the interior FEM problems.
infographic.watch_item: Choosing when to omit BEM corrections requires care, because small exterior corrections remain relevant at weakly damped frequencies.
infographic.paper_title: An all-steps-at-once algorithm for time-domain wave propagation in heterogeneous and unbounded media

title: Learning inadequacy of Bayesian neural operators for PDE-constrained inference and design
authors: Pratyush Kumar Singh, Lianghao Cao, E. Bruce Pitman, Danial Faghihi
abstract: Partial differential equations (PDEs) underpin predictive modeling across science, engineering and medicine. Their use in digital twins, parameter inference and optimal design requires repeated solutions across parameters and scenarios. For nonlinear, transient and multiphysics systems, these calculations can make numerical simulation prohibitively expensive. Here we introduce the residual-informed Bayesian neural operator (RI-BNO), which learns operator inadequacy using a posteriori error estimates from the governing PDEs and incorporates its correction and uncertainty into Bayesian training and prediction. We establish local error bounds for the residual-informed estimates under stability and smoothness assumptions. We demonstrate RI-BNO on a non-linear reaction-diffusion benchmark with DeepONet and latent-subspace architectures, Markov chain Monte Carlo inference of glioma parameter fields from magnetic resonance imaging, and Monte Carlo risk-averse optimization of three-dimensional thermal breaks in building envelopes under manufacturing uncertainty. Across the evaluated examples, RI-BNO improves agreement with finite element (FE) reference predictions, parameter posteriors and optimized designs while using half as many full nonlinear or transient training simulations as the vanilla Bayesian neural operator (vBNO). For thermal break design, online optimization time decreases from 178 hours with the FE model to 18 minutes with RI-BNO. These results demonstrate the value of explicit inadequacy modeling in neural operators for reliable PDE-based inference and design.

infographic.key_insight: Residual-informed Bayesian neural operators learn and quantify surrogate inadequacy using PDE-based error estimates, improving inference and design with fewer full-order training simulations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: More reliable PDE surrogates can accelerate digital twins, parameter estimation and risk-averse engineering design without ignoring surrogate error.
method: Estimate operator inadequacy from governing-PDE residuals using a posteriori error estimates.
Incorporate inadequacy correction and uncertainty into Bayesian training and prediction.
Establish local error bounds under stability and smoothness assumptions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across reaction–diffusion, glioma inference and 3D thermal-break design examples, RI-BNO improved agreement with FE references using half as many full nonlinear or transient training simulations as vanilla BNO; thermal-break online optimization fell from 178 hours with FE to 18 minutes.
infographic.watch_item: Error guarantees are local and depend on stability and smoothness assumptions; reliability beyond the evaluated regimes requires validation.
infographic.paper_title: Learning inadequacy of Bayesian neural operators for PDE-constrained inference and design

title: Long-time asymptotics of advection-diffusion of finite element differential forms
authors: Kaibo Hu, Jindong Wang, Umberto Zerbinati
abstract: This paper establishes global numerical analysis for the long-time behavior of Lie advection--diffusion of differential forms discretized by finite element exterior calculus (FEEC). For potential flows we prove a weighted Hodge decomposition implying convergence to harmonic forms of dimension equal to the Betti number, yielding a differential-form antidynamo theorem. For general advection, a mixed FEEC scheme is introduced and shown to preserve key structural properties: the dimension of closed stationary discrete $k$-forms is at least $b_k$. Under verified spectral-preservation assumptions (satisfied for small $h$ by spectral approximation and for arbitrary $h$ by a lowest-order exponential-fitting $M$-matrix discretization), discrete antidynamo theorems are obtained. In particular, on two-dimensional manifolds the numerical $1$-forms converge exponentially to a uniquely determined closed stationary form for every diffusion coefficient $η>0$, rigorously excluding spurious dynamo growth. The results guarantee that FEEC faithfully inherits the topological long-time asymptotics of the continuous system.

infographic.key_insight: Structure-preserving finite element discretizations retain topology-controlled long-time behavior of advected differential forms and, under spectral-preservation conditions, exclude spurious dynamo growth.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These guarantees support reliable long-duration advection–diffusion simulations where artificial growth or incorrect steady states would undermine predictions.
method: Use a weighted Hodge decomposition to characterize potential-flow limits through harmonic forms and Betti numbers.
Construct a mixed finite element exterior calculus scheme that preserves closed stationary modes.
Establish discrete antidynamo results using spectral approximation or lowest-order exponential-fitting M-matrix discretization.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports analytical guarantees, including exponential convergence of numerical 1-forms on two-dimensional manifolds for every positive diffusion coefficient, rather than empirical benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Discrete antidynamo guarantees require spectral preservation; arbitrary-mesh validity is established for the specified lowest-order exponential-fitting discretization, not generic FEEC schemes.
infographic.paper_title: Long-time asymptotics of advection-diffusion of finite element differential forms

title: A scaling law for numerical computation of fracture stress intensity factors
authors: Ronghao Cui, Jan Martin Nordbotten, Ivar Stefansson, Inga Berre
abstract: Numerical simulations of fracture propagation require accurate computation of stress intensity factors (SIFs) to determine whether a pre-existing fracture will propagate. Even though displacement solutions from well-established numerical methods generally converge with mesh refinement, the convergence behavior of SIF estimates remains less understood. In this work, we propose a scaling law to improve the performance of SIF extraction using two-point displacement correlation methods. This scaling law relates sampling distance from the fracture tip to mesh resolution. It is developed by balancing the asymptotic truncation error against the numerical discretization error. Three numerical discretization methods--standard quadratic finite elements, quadratic finite elements with quarter-point elements, and a multi-point stress approximation finite volume method--are employed to validate the proposed scaling law on fracture benchmark problems under pure-mode and mixed-mode loading. We find that the conventional nearest-tip sampling strategy fails to compute convergent SIF estimates. In contrast, the proposed scaling-based approach yields decreasing errors in the SIF estimates as the mesh is refined. Across all three discretization methods, the proposed scaling law captures the sampling locations required for convergent SIF extraction, suggesting a general numerical characteristic of near-tip SIF extraction.

infographic.key_insight: Linking fracture-tip sampling distance to mesh resolution enables convergent stress intensity factor estimates where conventional nearest-tip sampling fails.
infographic.engineering_relevance: More reliable stress intensity factors support fracture-propagation decisions in computational solid mechanics.
method: Extract stress intensity factors using two-point displacement correlation.
Derive a sampling-distance scaling law by balancing asymptotic truncation and numerical discretization errors.
Validate with quadratic finite elements, quarter-point finite elements, and multi-point stress approximation finite volumes.
infographic.evidence_signal: On pure-mode and mixed-mode fracture benchmarks, scaling-based sampling produced decreasing errors under mesh refinement across all three methods, unlike nearest-tip sampling.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not specify the scaling formula or its parameters, so implementation requires consulting the full paper.
infographic.paper_title: A scaling law for numerical computation of fracture stress intensity factors

title: Using an instrumented hammer to predict the lateral hinge fracture in high tibial osteotomy: A cadaveric study
authors: Claire Bastard, Manon Bas-Dit Nugues, Giuseppe Rosi, Charles-Henri Flouzat-Lachaniette, Arnaud Dubory, Guillaume Haiat
abstract: Open-wedge High-Tibial Osteotomy is the most commonly employed technique addressing varus knee osteoarthritis. During this procedure, the osteotome passes through cortical and trabecular bone. A common complication is lateral hinge fractures, which depends upon when the surgeon stops impacting the osteotome. The aim of the present study is to determine whether an instrumented hammer can be employed to detect (i) the bone type (cortical or trabecular) surrounding the osteotome tip and (ii) when bone is fractured by the osteotome. Seventeen lower-limb specimens were obtained from nine fresh human anatomical subjects. The osteotome was impacted using the instrumented hammer until rupture. Each impact signal was recorded and analyzed. An algorithm was developed to detect the transitions between cortical and trabecular bone and vice versa. Detection was based on the relative variation of $τ$ derived from the force signal as a function of time as the time difference between the second___and___first impact peaks. The values of $τ$ were significantly lower in cortical bone compared to trabecular bone. Considering the arrival of the osteotome tip in trabecular bone during a medial, a difference of less than 2 impacts between the surgeon and the algorithm was obtained for 71% of the cases. For the lateral osteotomy it was obtained in 81% of the cases. This cadaveric study demonstrated that the instrumented hammer could prevent impacts leading to hinge rupture, which suggests that future clinical trials are warranted.

infographic.key_insight: Timing between force-signal peaks from an instrumented hammer distinguished cortical from trabecular bone and showed potential to warn against impacts causing lateral hinge fracture.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Impact-force monitoring could provide intraoperative feedback to help surgeons stop osteotome advancement before hinge rupture during open-wedge high tibial osteotomy.
method: Record hammer force–time signals during osteotome impacts until bone rupture.
Calculate τ, the time interval between the first and second impact peaks.
Use relative changes in τ to detect transitions between cortical and trabecular bone.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 17 lower-limb specimens from nine cadaveric donors, τ was significantly lower in cortical bone; algorithm–surgeon differences in identifying trabecular entry were under two impacts in 71% of medial and 81% of lateral osteotomies.
infographic.watch_item: Clinical validation is needed: cadaveric transition-detection results do not establish reliable fracture prevention in patients.
infographic.paper_title: Using an instrumented hammer to predict the lateral hinge fracture in high tibial osteotomy: A cadaveric study

title: Baryonic Keys and the Inheritance of Crypto-Assets: Revisiting the Tales From the Crypt Protocol
authors: Frédéric Prost
abstract: The inheritance of crypto-assets faces a structural obstacle: ownership is the knowledge of a key, so the key either disappears with its owner or has to be shared beforehand. The Tales From the Crypt Protocol (TFCP) addressed one part of the problem, the distributed and privacy-preserving acknowledgment of a death by a blockchain. We revisit it with a new primitive. A \emph{baryonic key} is a physical object from which bits are obtained only through a measurement, are never stored digitally, and which exists in exactly $n$ copies, where $n$ is neither zero nor unbounded. We define the primitive, outline a candidate instantiation based on a replicated micro-fractured relief, and state its limits: digitising a copy is slow and tamper-evident, not impossible. We also outline other uses of the primitive, from post-quantum pre-shared keys to common coins for Byzantine agreement. We then give a threat model for TFCP, review the attack models of the literature that apply to it, and show where it resists and where it does not. We propose TFCP-B, in which decrypting the will requires both a secret shared among registrars and the response of a baryonic key, and in which heirs claim their share through hash commitments, without any prior key or wallet. We detail each change from TFCP to TFCP-B, with its rationale and its price. TFCP-B removes the anonymity loss caused by colluding registrars and blocks several false-alarm attacks. It does not remove the shallow-account attack, remains exposed to transaction censorship during the deliberation period, and introduces new assumptions on custodians and reading devices. The security arguments are informal and the physical figures are design estimates.

infographic.key_insight: TFCP-B combines physically measured baryonic keys with registrar-held secret shares to strengthen crypto-asset inheritance without requiring heirs to hold prior keys or wallets.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A proposed replicated micro-fractured relief links physical surface measurement and tamper evidence to cryptographic access control.
method: Define a baryonic key as a physical object with a finite, nonzero number of copies whose bits are obtained through measurement.
Require both a registrar-shared secret and a baryonic-key response to decrypt the will.
Use hash commitments for heir claims and analyze TFCP-B against inheritance-protocol threats.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports informal security arguments and physical design estimates, not experimentally validated performance.
infographic.watch_item: Digitization is slow and tamper-evident rather than impossible; custodian and reader assumptions, shallow-account attacks, and transaction censorship remain concerns.
infographic.paper_title: Baryonic Keys and the Inheritance of Crypto-Assets: Revisiting the Tales From the Crypt Protocol

title: Explicit topology control in isogeometric topology optimization using persistent homology
authors: Wenliang Yin, Gengchen Li, Hongwei Lin
abstract: Explicitly controlling structural topology remains a major challenge in topology optimization. While many implicit methods regulate topology only indirectly, available explicit strategies often focus on two-dimensional hole control or extend to 3D without a unified treatment of tunnels and cavities. This study proposes a differentiable, persistent homology-based framework for explicit topology control in 2D and 3D isogeometric topology optimization. A NURBS-represented density field induces a single sublevel filtration whose persistence diagrams quantify the connected components, holes in 2D, and tunnels and cavities in 3D directly. To enforce prescribed bounds on topological feature counts, weighted topological objectives are applied in a staged manner that coordinates the different homology dimensions. Each redundant feature is removed either by cutting or by filling according to the region of its corresponding persistence pair, avoiding the excessive structural changes associated with filling alone. The topological inverse mapping yields analytical sensitivities with respect to the density control coefficients, so that the resulting objective is readily incorporated into gradient-based optimization and solved by the method of moving asymptotes. Numerical experiments on 2D and 3D benchmarks demonstrate explicit and reliable topology control while maintaining competitive mechanical performance and stable convergence.

infographic.key_insight: Persistent homology enables explicit control of connected components, holes, tunnels, and cavities in 2D and 3D isogeometric topology optimization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Engineers can prescribe topology bounds while seeking mechanically competitive structural designs.
method: Compute persistence diagrams from a single sublevel filtration of a NURBS density field.
Apply staged, weighted topological objectives and remove redundant features by cutting or filling.
Derive analytical density-control sensitivities through topological inverse mapping and optimize using the method of moving asymptotes.
infographic.evidence_signal: Reported 2D and 3D benchmark experiments demonstrate reliable topology control, competitive mechanical performance, and stable convergence.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify computational overhead or sensitivity to the staged objective weights.
infographic.paper_title: Explicit topology control in isogeometric topology optimization using persistent homology

title: Machine learning of strength surfaces enables high regularization length phase-field fracture
authors: S Chockalingam, Aditya Kumar, Adrian Buganza Tepole
abstract: Classical phase-field models of brittle fracture capture toughness-controlled crack growth but not the material's strength surface, which governs crack nucleation. The theory of Kumar et al. (2020) incorporates the strength surface through a nucleation driving force, and Chockalingam (2025) derived this driving force for arbitrary strength surfaces described by $n$ material parameters, with which the phase-field strength surface (PFSS) converges to the material strength surface as the regularization length $\varepsilon \to 0$ and matches it exactly at $n$ chosen states for any $\varepsilon$. In practice, however, the strength surface must be supplied as an analytic form chosen and calibrated case by case, and for the widely used analytic surfaces ($n=2$) accurate strength reproduction requires $\varepsilon$ commensurate with the Irwin characteristic length $l_{ch}$, imposing prohibitive mesh requirements for large structures. We introduce a neural-network (NN) strength function that is learned directly from strength data, is physics-constrained by construction, and provides far more calibration parameters than analytic surfaces; the calibration is generalized to any number of strength states and to enforce openness in chosen directions. A single architecture captures synthetic data from the Mohr-Coulomb, Drucker-Prager, Mogi-Coulomb and 3D Hoek-Brown surfaces and experimental data for graphite, natural rubber and styrene-butadiene rubber. The resulting PFSS is accurate up to $\varepsilon = 10\,l_{ch}$, whereas that of the exact analytic surfaces performs comparatively poorly even at $\varepsilon = 0.5\,l_{ch}$. Finite-element simulations validate the theory across fracture regimes. By decoupling strength fidelity from the regularization length, the approach substantially reduces the mesh resolution required for phase-field fracture simulations of large structures.

infographic.key_insight: A physics-constrained neural-network strength function preserves phase-field strength accuracy at regularization lengths up to 10 times the Irwin characteristic length.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Decoupling strength fidelity from regularization length enables coarser meshes, reducing computational demands for fracture simulations of large structures.
method: Learn the material strength function directly from data using a physics-constrained neural network.
Incorporate the learned function into the phase-field crack-nucleation driving force.
Generalize calibration to multiple strength states and enforce openness in selected directions.
infographic.evidence_signal: One architecture fits four synthetic strength surfaces and experimental data for graphite and two rubbers; finite-element simulations validate the theory across fracture regimes.
infographic.watch_item: Reliable deployment still requires representative strength data and validation for the target material and loading conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Machine learning of strength surfaces enables high regularization length phase-field fracture

title: A mesh-free deep energy method for phase-field modeling of thermally driven brittle fracture
authors: Han Zhang, Mehrisadat Makki Alamdari, Babak Shahbodagh, Mohammad Vahab, Cosmin Anitescu, Timon Rabczuk
abstract: Phase-field simulation of thermally driven fracture requires resolving localized crack bands whose paths are unknown in advance and thermal boundary layers whose thickness evolves during the transient. Neural energy-based computations of thermal fracture have so far started from defects placed in advance. This paper proposes a mesh-free deep energy method based on multiresolution neural representations that predicts spontaneous crack nucleation, crack spacing, and selective crack propagation and arrest under transient thermal loading. Two networks, each with its own multiresolution encoding, represent the displacement and phase fields and the transient temperature, and the mechanical energy and the incremental functional of the backward Euler heat equation are estimated on integration points redrawn at every iteration. Restricting irreversibility to the crack set, carrying the optimizer state across load steps and decaying the learning rates within each step help prevent spurious damage accumulation. On two notched plates the initiation peak loads agree closely with an independent finite element reference. On a quenched glass strip under an analytical temperature field the crack path changes from straight to oscillatory and then to branched, with an oscillation threshold close to the linear stability prediction. Under a prescribed boundary temperature a quenched ceramic slab forms a crack array of the type observed in experiment, with a spacing close to that of a published benchmark. On the slab and a quenched annulus the arrays are denser than those of a finite element computation on the same material field. No crack paths, nucleation sites or crack-adapted meshes are prescribed.

infographic.key_insight: A mesh-free deep energy method predicts thermally driven crack nucleation, spacing, propagation and arrest without prescribing crack paths or nucleation sites.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports thermal-shock fracture analysis where evolving thermal boundary layers and unknown crack paths complicate mesh-based simulation.
method: Separate multiresolution neural representations model displacement and phase fields, and transient temperature.
Minimize mechanical energy and a backward Euler thermal functional using integration points resampled each iteration.
Restrict irreversibility to the crack set, retain optimizer state across load steps and decay learning rates within each step.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests show close agreement with finite element initiation peak loads on two notched plates, a glass-strip oscillation threshold near linear stability predictions and ceramic-slab crack spacing near a published benchmark.
infographic.watch_item: Crack arrays in the slab and annulus are denser than finite element predictions on the same material field, leaving a discrepancy that warrants further validation.
infographic.paper_title: A mesh-free deep energy method for phase-field modeling of thermally driven brittle fracture
